summary.text: At \(n=1\), the single summand has \(\beta(0)=t(0)=1\), so \(a(1)=8/2=4\). But \(1=2^0\) is a power of two while \(4\) is even, contradicting the claimed parity equivalence.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\beta(k)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{2}\binom{k+j}{j}
\]
be the Apéry-number factor, and let
\[
t(k)=[x^k](x^2+4x-1)^k
\]
be the coefficient of \(x^k\) in \((x^2+4x-1)^k\). The sequence in the conjecture is
\[
a(n)=\frac{1}{2n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^k(15k+8)\beta(k)t(k)
\qquad(n>0).
\]
We disprove the asserted parity characterization by taking \(n=1\).

First compute all the quantities occurring in the sum. Since the sum defining \(\beta(0)\) has only the index \(j=0\),
\[
\beta(0)=\binom00^2\binom00=1.
\]
Also,
\[
(x^2+4x-1)^0=1,
\]
so the coefficient of \(x^0\) is
\[
t(0)=1.
\]
For \(n=1\), the weighted sum has only the index \(k=0\). Consequently its sole summand is
\[
(-1)^0(15\cdot0+8)\beta(0)t(0)
=1\cdot8\cdot1\cdot1
=8.
\]
The normalizing denominator is \(2n=2\). Hence
\[
a(1)=\frac{8}{2}=4.
\]
(In particular, the integrality part of the conjecture happens to hold at this value; it is the claimed parity equivalence that fails.)

The integer \(4\) is even, since \(4=2\cdot2\), and therefore it is not odd. On the other hand, \(1\) is a positive power of two in the usual sense relevant here, because
\[
1=2^0.
\]
Thus, at the positive integer \(n=1\), the assertion “\(a(n)\) is odd” is false while the assertion “\(n\) is a power of two” is true. Therefore the claimed equivalence
\[
a(n)\text{ is odd}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\text{ is a power of two}
\]
fails at \(n=1\). Since the conjecture requires this equivalence (together with integrality) for every integer \(n>0\), this single counterexample disproves it.
